articles.title: Everything Kate Middleton Has Shared About Her Cancer Diagnosis
articles.summary: Catherine, Princess of Wales is now in remission from cancer, a diagnosis she shared in a 2024 video. She's now returned to royal duties.
articles.body: Following months of speculation about her wellbeing, in 2024, Catherine, Princess of Wales, revealed she was diagnosed with cancer. The former Kate Middleton has since shared that she completed treatment and is now in remission. She's also taken on public royal duties after pausing them for several months due to her health. Many people have wondered what kind of cancer the princess had, as it was discovered during an abdominal surgery, but Buckingham Palace has not publicly shared those details. That said, Kate has begun sharing regular updates about her treatment and state of her health. She first revealed her cancer diagnosis in March 2024, sharing that she'd be undergoing chemotherapy. Her next update came in June of that year, when she said she was receiving chemo and made her first public appearance in months, at Trooping the Colour. In September 2024, the mother of three confirmed she'd finished chemotherapy, calling herself "cancer free." In January 2025, she announced she was in remission. "It is a relief to now be in remission and I remain focused on recovery. As anyone who has experienced a cancer diagnosis will know, it takes time to adjust to a new normal. I am however looking forward to a fulfilling year ahead. There is much to look forward to. Thank you to everyone for your continued support. C," she wrote on Instagram. Since completing treatment, Kate had been candid about the struggles she's faced since. “You have to find your new normal and that takes time...and it’s a roller coaster," she said in July 2025 while visiting hospital patients. In a new documentary called “Heal,” premiering on NBC on Nov. 30 at 8 p.m. ET and streaming on Peacock Dec. 1, Kate reflects on her cancer journey as she hikes and summits three of the tallest peaks in Scotland, England and Wales within 24 hours. Along the trail, she contemplates recovery, “how to reconnect with the things you once knew and how to find a sense of hope and joy alongside uncertainty,” she says in the documentary trailer. Ahead is a complete timeline of Kate Middleton's cancer journey, including every health update she and the palace have shared. A Timeline of Kate Middleton’s Cancer Journey December 2023 The princess’s last public appearance before her cancer diagnosis came in late 2023 during her family's annual Christmas church outing at the Church of St. Mary Magdalene in Sandringham, near one of the king’s royal estates. January 2024 Kensington Palace announced that Kate had undergone “planned abdominal surgery” in mid-January. She was discharged from London Clinic, a private hospital, 13 days later. At the time, the palace said that Kate would be recuperating for two to three months after her surgery (before her cancer diagnosis) and that her husband, Prince William, would be postponing appearances in the coming months while his wife recovered. Kate also had to cancel and postpone multiple engagements. Kate returned home to Windsor to continue to recover in late January, according to a palace statement, which added, “She is making good progress.” For weeks after the surgery and before her cancer diagnosis was revealed, speculation, rumors and conspiracies swirled around the wellbeing of the future queen. The palace has yet to reveal what the abdominal surgery was meant to address. February 2024 William pulled out of attending his godfather’s memorial service due to a “personal matter.” Kensington Palace later confirmed the prince did not attend the service due to his wife’s cancer diagnosis. In late February, as rumors about Kate's health and whereabouts mounted, the palace issued another statement about her recovery, explaining that her absence from the public eye shouldn’t be unexpected. March 2024 In a March 2024 video statement, the Princess of Wales revealed that she was in the “early stages” of preventative chemotherapy after being diagnosed with cancer. Preventive (also known as adjuvant) chemotherapy follows any initial interventions, such as surgery, to prevent cancer from returning. Clinical trials have found that chemotherapy can reduce the risk of the cancer recurring. Kate did not specify the kind of cancer that she had. The diagnosis came after Kate underwent major abdominal surgery in January. “At the time, it was thought that my condition was noncancerous,” she said in the video. “The surgery was successful. However, tests after the operation found cancer had been present.” Kate added that the news of her cancer diagnosis came as a “huge shock,” noting that she and William were aiming to “manage this privately for the sake of our young family.” “As you can imagine, this has taken time. It has taken me time to recover from major surgery in order to start my treatment,” she said. “But, most importantly, it has taken us time to explain everything to George, Charlotte and Louis in a way that is appropriate for them, and to reassure them that I am going to be OK.” The princess assured viewers in the video that she is “well and getting stronger every day.” She also asked for “time, space and privacy” as she undergoes treatment and said she is focused on making a “full recovery.” April 2024 William returned to royal duties in mid-April. May 2024 During a mid-May appearance, William shared a vague update on Kate's health when visiting St. Mary’s Community Hospital in the U.K. “He said, ‘She’s doing well, thanks,’” hospital administrator Tracy Smith told reporters, according to the Associated Press. In late May, a senior palace aide said the princess has not returned to royal duties, though she was engaged in an early childhood initiative in the U.K. The Royal Foundation Business Taskforce for Early Childhood released a report earlier in May, and the future queen took time to review it, according to a spokesperson. June 2024 On June 14, Kate released her first remarks on her cancer treatment since revealing her diagnosis in March. She shared that she was "not out of the woods" with her treatment and that she still has "a few more months" of chemotherapy left to go. “I am making good progress, but as anyone going through chemotherapy will know, there are good days and bad days. On those bad days you feel weak, tired and you have to give in to your body resting. But on the good days, when you feel stronger, you want to make the most of feeling well,” she said. Read her full remarks. On June 15, Kate made her first public appearance since her diagnosis at Trooping the Colour, an annual ceremony celebrating the king's birthday. July 2024 The princess was well enough to make her second public appearance since announcing her cancer diagnosis, when she attended the men’s singles final on the 14th day of Wimbledon. She received a standing ovation when she entered the Royal Box with daughter Princess Charlotte. September 2024 The princess revealed that she is done with chemotherapy. “Doing what I can to stay cancer free is now my focus. Although I have finished chemotherapy, my path to healing and full recovery is long and I must continue to take each day as it comes.” “I am however looking forward to being back at work and undertaking a few more public engagements in the coming months when I can,” she wrote on social media. The following week, she attended an official engagement at Windsor Castle on early years education in the U.K. October 2024 Kate made her first public appearance since announcing that she'd finished her cancer treatment. She and William met with emergency responders and parents of victims of a July knife attack in Southport, England. January 2025 Kate announced she's in remission from cancer. In an Instagram post celebrating her new role as a joint patron of The Royal Marsden NHS Foundation Trust with Prince William on Jan. 14, the princess shared the update about her health. She is still adjusting to "a new normal," she wrote. That same day, Kate also visited patients at the Royal Marsden, the London hospital where she received cancer treatment. She shared photos of the visit on the social media platform and thanked the hospital staff for the care she received. "I wanted to take the opportunity to say thank you to The Royal Marsden for looking after me so well during the past year," Kate wrote. "My heartfelt thanks goes to all those who have quietly walked alongside William and me as we have navigated everything. We couldn’t have asked for more. The care and advice we have received throughout my time as a patient has been exceptional." During her visit, Kate shared details about her own cancer treatment, calling chemotherapy "really tough," according to U.K. news agency PA. Her treatment was delivered through a port, a device implanted into the skin, which she says she became attached to. When it came time to remove it, she admitted she hesitated. Ahead of treatment, she revealed those around her urged her to "please keep a positive mindset," adding that it made "such a difference." Of its newest patron, Dame Cally Palmer, chief executive of The Royal Marsden NHS Foundation Trust, said in a statement, “we are incredibly fortunate to receive Royal Patronage — it is inspiring for staff and patients and enables us to shine a light on the outstanding work our staff deliver every day for patients and their families." April 2025 In a special short film, Kate discussed her relationship with nature and what it means to her to spend time outside. While on an outing with young scouts and their troop leader, she said, "I find it a very spiritual, and very intense, emotional reconnection, I suppose, these environments." Nature is a place for her to balance and find peace in a busy world, she added. The princess echoed this sentiment a few months prior in a Feb. 2025 Instagram post she shared on World Cancer Day. In the photo, taken by her son Prince Louis, Kate stands with her arms outstretched in a forest. "Don’t forget to nurture all that which lies beyond the disease. C #WorldCancerDay," she wrote as her caption. On April 29, in honor of her 14th anniversary of her wedding to Prince William, the pair traveled to the Isle of Mull off the west coast of Scotland for two days. They shared a video featuring the island's natural beauty and, in the caption, wrote they look forward to "exploring how islanders are protecting their natural world." While there, Kate and Prince William spent time in Ardura Community Forest. On Instagram, the couple called the experience "A powerful reminder of the importance of protecting the environment and the role outdoor learning plays in building connection and care for nature." In other posts, they celebrated the region's resilience, resourcefulness and sense of community in working toward a greater good. May 2025 In a May 2025 interview with The Times, Kate's brother, James Middleton, spoke about his sister's cancer diagnosis. “What I think is that, as a family, you learn to see and process and understand things. For her and her family it was a challenging time, and I know for us and our bigger family it was a challenging time, but I think it’s about communication and it’s about offering support and help where you can,” he said. He also spoke to what that support should look like. “Being there for someone is such an important part, and it doesn’t necessarily have to be on your terms and it shouldn’t be on your terms. It should be on their terms; unconditional: ‘I’m not doing it for something in return. I’m doing it because I love you.’ And that’s the simplest way of really demonstrating love. You can do it in all these various fancy ways but actually, you know, it is just generally being there.” July 2025 During an appearance at an Essex hospital, Kate spoke about how tough life after treatment has been. “You put on a sort of brave face (with) stoicism through treatment. (When) treatment’s done, then it’s like, ‘I can crack on, get back to normal again,’” she said, per video footage from the BBC. During her conversation with patients, Kate admitted it was difficult to adjust to normal life. “But actually, the phase afterwards is really difficult. You’re not necessarily under the clinical team any longer, but you’re not able to function normally at home as you perhaps once used to,” she said. But she shared that she gave herself grace. “You have to find your new normal, and that takes time,” she said. Kate went on to describe the period after treatment as a “rollercoaster.” “It’s not one smooth plane, which you expect it to be. But the reality is it’s not. You go through hard times,” she said. During her visit, Kate also planted a single pink flower dubbed Catherine's Rose at the RHS Wellbeing Garden in Colchester. In an Instagram post, the princess described the moment as "a gesture rooted in hope and care." "Grateful to spend time with NHS staff and volunteers tending this space, and to see the rose incorporated into gardens supporting recovery and reflection across the UK," she added in her caption. March 2026 During a visit to a beer hall with Prince William, Kate revealed she avoids alcohol. When asked if she's much of a beer drinker, the royal responded, "No, actually, since my diagnosis, drinking alcohol is not really something — it's something I have to be a lot more conscious of now," she said in a video posted on YouTube. May 2026 Kate traveled to Italy for her first international trip since her recovery. An aide to the princess told NBC News, “She’s looking forward to being here, she’s energised, she’s enthused, she’s excited to see Reggio Emilia in action and meet the people here too,” referring to the early childhood education curriculum the princess would be observing. “This is a global mission,” the aide went on. “She wants to look at other [early childhood] models around the world and really create a global conversation.” “This is a huge moment for the princess. There will be many highlights of 2026 but this being her first international visit post her recovery... this is a really significant moment for her.” On Instagram, the princess shared her thoughts about an assembly she sat in on. “Joining the morning assembly at Scuola Salvador Allende, listening as children share what they want to explore, build, and discover together as part of the Reggio Emilia Approach,” the caption reads. She and the children spent time in the garden, where Kate said learning, connection and play take place. In the Reggio Emilia Approach, nature is the “third teacher” working alongside school teachers and caregivers, the caption went on. July 2026 In a physical feat, Kate hiked three mountains in 24 hours. When she was recovering in the hospital two years earlier, James Middleton, Kate’s brother, said vowed to complete the National Three Peaks Challenge with her, and so they did. The pair hiked a mountain in Scotland, another in England and the third in Wales. On Instagram, the royal revealed she took on the challenge in honor of The Royal Marsden Cancer Charity which supports cancer programs and research. November 2026 On Nov. 30, Kate will give a close-up look at her experience taking on the National Three Peaks Challenge in a documentary that will air on NBC and stream on Peacock. In it, Kate reveals what she’s learned since completing treatment and what that means for her life moving forward. “Often it is through pain that we realize there’s a great beauty that lies beyond that,” Kate says in the documentary trailer. All proceeds from the film will go to The Royal Marsden Cancer Charity, according to Kate and William’s joint Instagram account. What Type of Cancer Does Kate Middleton Have? The princess has not specified what kind of cancer she was undergoing treatment for. She shared that it was discovered after an abdominal surgery in January. The most common types of cancer discovered through abdominal surgery are gastrointestinal, such as colon or stomach, genital or urinary, Dr. Ben Ho Park, director of precision oncology at Vanderbilt School of Medicine, previously told TODAY.com. He was sure to point out, however, that “it could be anything.” Has Kate Returned to Her Royal Duties? Yes. Kate attended her first official engagement after being diagnosed with cancer in mid-September 2024, a meeting on early years education in the U.K. Then, in mid-October 2024, she made her first public appearance since finishing cancer treatment: She met with the parents of a child killed in a knife attack in northwest England. She and William were photographed speaking with emergency responders. A senior palace aide previously told NBC News in late May: “(Kate) will return to work when she has the green light from her doctors. She needs her space and the privacy to recover right now.”

articles.title: Após cirurgia no coração e 95 dias internada, idosa recebe alta em MT | G1
articles.standfirst: Aos 63 anos, Ozana Oribes passou por uma cirurgia cardíaca com três procedimentos e enfrentou complicações. Ainda acamada, precisa de ajuda para continuar a recuperação.
articles.summary: Aos 63 anos, Ozana Oribes passou por uma cirurgia cardíaca com três procedimentos e enfrentou complicações. Ainda acamada, precisa de ajuda para continuar a recuperação.
articles.body:

Após 95 dias internada, Ozana Pires de Camargo Oribes , de 63 anos, recebeu alta do Hospital Central, em Cuiabá , no dia 12 de novembro. Ela passou por uma cirurgia no coração e enfrentou complicações durante o período de internação, antes de comemorar a alta médica.

A saída foi marcada por uma homenagem da equipe médica, que entregou à paciente um certificado de bravura. Em vídeo, Ozana aparece deixando o hospital enquanto comemora com os profissionais de saúde (assista acima) .

A família mora em Nobres , a 151 km de Cuiabá, onde começou a sequência de problemas de saúde enfrentada pela idosa. Segundo a filha, Maria Camargo, o primeiro infarto aconteceu no Dia das Mães, em maio deste ano, enquanto os familiares preparavam um almoço para comemorar a data.

Ozana foi levada a um hospital e depois transferida para uma unidade em Nova Mutum , onde aguardava uma cirurgia cardíaca. O procedimento estava previsto para 26 de maio, mas, no dia anterior, o marido dela morreu em Nobres. A paciente voltou para casa para acompanhar o funeral e, depois do enterro, sofreu outro infarto, segundo a filha.

Em 9 de agosto, ela foi encaminhada ao Hospital Central, em Cuiabá. De acordo com o resumo de alta fornecido pela família, a cirurgia foi realizada no dia 19 daquele mês e envolveu três intervenções: ampliação do anel da válvula aórtica, substituição da válvula por uma prótese biológica e revascularização do coração.

Maria contou que a mãe sofreu uma parada cardíaca durante a cirurgia e precisou ser intubada. Depois, foi levada para a Unidade de Terapia Intensiva (UTI), onde teve outra parada cardíaca no mesmo dia. Na ocasião, os médicos alertaram a família sobre a gravidade do quadro.

O documento hospitalar também registra outras complicações durante a internação, como acidente vascular cerebral (AVC), problemas respiratórios associados a um quadro de edema pulmonar e infecções urinárias recorrentes.

A filha contou que a família chegou a acreditar que não teria a mãe de volta. O medo era perder os dois pais no mesmo ano, já que o pai havia morrido em maio.

“A gente achou que ia perder nosso pai e nossa mãe no mesmo ano. Teve um momento em que pensamos que ela não voltaria para casa. Mas graças a Deus, ela sobreviveu”, relatou.

Em casa, Ozana ainda está acamada e precisa usar fraldas, tomar medicamentos e fazer fisioterapia para continuar a recuperação. A família afirma que não tem condições de arcar com todos os custos e pede ajuda para manter os cuidados.

“Que Deus possa tocar no coração dessas pessoas, possa estar ajudando elas, ajudando a gente, na verdade”, pediu.

articles.title: Câncer de próstata: estudo avalia vigilância em casos de baixo risco | G1
articles.standfirst: Hospital Erasto Gaertner participa de pesquisa multicêntrica apresentada no Congresso Brasileiro de Oncologia Clínica e reconhecida com o Prêmio SBOC de Ciências.
articles.summary: Hospital Erasto Gaertner participa de pesquisa multicêntrica apresentada no Congresso Brasileiro de Oncologia Clínica e reconhecida com o Prêmio SBOC de Ciências.
articles.body:
O câncer de próstata é um dos principais tipos de câncer entre os homens e envolve diferentes possibilidades de acompanhamento e tratamento, de acordo com as características de cada paciente. Entre as estratégias utilizadas em casos selecionados de baixo risco está a vigilância ativa, abordagem que permite acompanhar a evolução da doença antes de indicar um tratamento definitivo.

No Brasil, compreender os resultados dessa estratégia dentro da realidade do Sistema Único de Saúde (SUS) é importante para avaliar sua segurança, seus resultados e os critérios que podem orientar a seleção dos pacientes. É nesse contexto que o Hospital Erasto Gaertner participa do VIGIASUS, estudo prospectivo e multicêntrico voltado à vigilância ativa do câncer de próstata no país.

O trabalho “Perda de PTEN por imuno-histoquímica e resultados da vigilância ativa no câncer de próstata de baixo risco: resultados da coorte multicêntrica brasileira VIGIASUS” teve entre seus autores o Dr. Murilo de Almeida Luz, cirurgião oncológico e urologista do Corpo Clínico do Hospital Erasto Gaertner.

O estudo foi apresentado na modalidade de apresentação oral durante o XXVII Congresso Brasileiro de Oncologia Clínica, realizado de 5 a 7 de novembro de 2026, no Windsor Oceânico, no Rio de Janeiro. A pesquisa recebeu o Prêmio SBOC de Ciências, reconhecimento concedido durante o congresso.

Prêmio SBOC. — Foto: Divulgação/Hospital Erasto Gaertner.

O que é vigilância ativa no câncer de próstata?

A vigilância ativa é uma estratégia utilizada principalmente em pacientes com câncer de próstata de baixo risco, nos quais a doença apresenta características que permitem um acompanhamento cuidadoso antes da realização de tratamentos definitivos.

Nesse modelo, o paciente permanece sob acompanhamento médico regular, com exames e avaliações periódicas que permitem monitorar a evolução da doença. Caso sejam identificadas mudanças que indiquem progressão ou maior risco, a equipe pode reavaliar a estratégia e indicar o tratamento mais adequado.

A proposta busca evitar ou adiar tratamentos desnecessários em pacientes selecionados, considerando que alguns tumores de próstata podem apresentar comportamento indolente. A definição da melhor conduta, porém, depende de avaliação individualizada e de critérios clínicos, laboratoriais, radiológicos e anatomopatológicos.

Por que estudar a vigilância ativa no Brasil?

Grande parte do conhecimento sobre vigilância ativa em câncer de próstata foi construída a partir de estudos realizados em outros países. Produzir evidências a partir da realidade brasileira permite compreender como essa estratégia se comporta em diferentes serviços e dentro das características do sistema de saúde do país.

É justamente essa uma das contribuições do VIGIASUS, estudo prospectivo que reúne diferentes centros brasileiros e acompanha pacientes incluídos em protocolos de vigilância ativa.

“Trata-se de um estudo prospectivo, multicêntrico, realizado em diferentes centros brasileiros, sobre vigilância ativa em câncer de próstata no Sistema Único de Saúde. No VIGIASUS, o Hospital Erasto Gaertner participa com uma quantidade significativa de pacientes, que tiveram a oportunidade de ser incluídos no estudo” , explica Dr. Murilo de Almeida Luz, cirurgião oncológico e urologista do Corpo Clínico do Hospital Erasto Gaertner.

O VIGIASUS é uma iniciativa do Hospital Moinhos de Vento, coordenada pelo Dr. Pedro Isaacson, que acompanha prospectivamente pacientes com câncer de próstata de baixo risco submetidos à estratégia de vigilância ativa em diferentes centros brasileiros.

O estudo busca produzir dados sobre o acompanhamento desses pacientes e avaliar características que possam contribuir para uma melhor compreensão da evolução da doença durante a vigilância ativa.

Entre os aspectos investigados está a presença de alterações relacionadas ao PTEN, gene envolvido em mecanismos importantes da biologia tumoral. No trabalho apresentado no Congresso Brasileiro de Oncologia Clínica, os pesquisadores avaliaram a perda de PTEN por imuno-histoquímica e sua relação com os resultados observados durante o acompanhamento dos pacientes.

A produção de evidências nacionais é especialmente relevante para ampliar o conhecimento sobre a vigilância ativa no contexto brasileiro e contribuir para decisões clínicas mais individualizadas.

A participação do Hospital Erasto Gaertner

Para o Hospital Erasto Gaertner, a participação no VIGIASUS representa uma oportunidade de contribuir com dados e experiência para uma pesquisa prospectiva e multicêntrica voltada à realidade do câncer de próstata no Brasil.

A presença do hospital no estudo também evidencia a atuação de seu corpo clínico na produção científica e na investigação de estratégias que podem contribuir para o aprimoramento da assistência oncológica.

A participação do Dr. Murilo de Almeida Luz no trabalho reforça uma trajetória de integração entre assistência, pesquisa, inovação e formação médica, construída ao longo de sua atuação no Hospital Erasto Gaertner.

Um estudo reconhecido no principal congresso de oncologia clínica do país

A apresentação do VIGIASUS ocorreu durante o XXVII Congresso Brasileiro de Oncologia Clínica, promovido pela Sociedade Brasileira de Oncologia Clínica (SBOC), que reuniu profissionais, pesquisadores e especialistas para discutir avanços e desafios da oncologia. A edição de 2026 foi realizada entre os dias 5 e 7 de novembro, no Rio de Janeiro.

O trabalho recebeu o Prêmio SBOC de Ciências e foi apresentado na modalidade oral, ampliando a visibilidade dos resultados da pesquisa e destacando a contribuição dos centros brasileiros envolvidos no VIGIASUS.

A premiação também representa um reconhecimento à produção científica desenvolvida por equipes que atuam na assistência e na pesquisa oncológica, aproximando o conhecimento produzido nos hospitais da prática clínica.

Da primeira cirurgia robótica às mil cirurgias

A trajetória do Dr. Murilo de Almeida Luz no Hospital Erasto Gaertner também está ligada à implantação da cirurgia robótica na instituição. Atualmente professor assistente de Oncologia Urológica na Icahn School of Medicine at Mount Sinai, nos Estados Unidos, o médico realizou a primeira cirurgia robótica do hospital e participou do início de uma trajetória que levou o programa a alcançar a marca de mil procedimentos.

Em maio de 2026, o Hospital Erasto Gaertner celebrou a realização de mil cirurgias robóticas, marco que simbolizou a evolução de um programa iniciado anos antes e ampliado com investimentos em tecnologia, capacitação e acesso aos pacientes.

No vídeo, gravado em maio deste ano, Dr. Murilo relembra o início da cirurgia robótica no Hospital Erasto Gaertner e a trajetória até a marca de mil procedimentos realizados pela instituição.

Curiosidade: quem realizou a primeira cirurgia robótica do Erasto?

O Dr. Murilo de Almeida Luz foi responsável pela realização da primeira cirurgia robótica do Hospital Erasto Gaertner. A partir desse início, o programa passou por diferentes etapas de desenvolvimento e chegou à marca de mil cirurgias robóticas realizadas pelo hospital.

A trajetória também esteve relacionada à formação de profissionais e à estruturação de um programa que ampliou o acesso à cirurgia robótica, incluindo pacientes atendidos pelo SUS.

Os treinamentos e simuladores utilizados pela Liga Paranaense de Combate ao Câncer foram viabilizados por meio de convênio com a Financiadora de Estudos e Projetos (FINEP), contribuindo para a capacitação das equipes e para o desenvolvimento do programa.

A participação do Hospital Erasto Gaertner no VIGIASUS mostra como a produção científica pode estar diretamente relacionada à assistência. Ao participar de uma pesquisa prospectiva e multicêntrica, o hospital contribui para a geração de conhecimento sobre uma estratégia de acompanhamento utilizada em pacientes selecionados com câncer de próstata de baixo risco.

O reconhecimento do trabalho no Congresso Brasileiro de Oncologia Clínica também destaca a importância da participação de instituições brasileiras na produção de evidências próprias e na discussão de estratégias que podem contribuir para o cuidado oncológico no país.

O Hospital Erasto Gaertner é referência em prevenção, diagnóstico e tratamento do câncer e integra a Liga Paranaense de Combate ao Câncer. A instituição oferece assistência oncológica especializada pelo Sistema Único de Saúde (SUS) e atua de forma integrada nas áreas de assistência, ensino, pesquisa e inovação.

articles.standfirst: Vítima tentou fazer uma ultrapassagem, perdeu o controle do veículo e bateu de frente com outra motocicleta na Avenida João Wallig.
articles.summary: O acidente de moto em Campina Grande ocorreu após Kleiton Olímpio derrapar em uma ultrapassagem na Avenida João Wallig e atingir outro veículo na manhã desta terça.
articles.body:
Motociclista de 37 anos morre após acidente entre duas motos em Campina Grande. — Foto: Reprodução/Redes Sociais

Um motociclista de 37 anos morreu após um acidente entre duas motos na manhã desta terça-feira (24), em Campina Grande , no Agreste da Paraíba. O acidente aconteceu por volta das 6h10, na Avenida João Wallig, no Distrito Industrial.

A vítima foi identificada como Kleiton Olímpio Amorim dos Santos . De acordo com a CPTran, Kleiton seguia pela avenida quando tentou fazer uma ultrapassagem, perdeu o controle da motocicleta e derrapou na pista.

Em seguida, a moto conduzida por ele bateu de frente com outra motocicleta, que trafegava no sentido contrário, na faixa de circulação correta. O segundo veículo era conduzido por Alan Wanderson Santos Dias .

Com o impacto, Kleiton caiu e sofreu ferimentos no rosto. Ele foi socorrido por uma equipe do Serviço de Atendimento Móvel de Urgência (Samu) e levado ao Hospital de Emergência e Trauma de Campina Grande. Segundo a unidade de saúde, o paciente passou por procedimentos médicos de emergência, mas não resistiu à gravidade dos ferimentos e morreu.

O condutor da outra motocicleta fez o teste do bafômetro, que apresentou resultado negativo para ingestão de álcool. Não foram divulgadas informações sobre o estado de saúde dele.

articles.title: Doença de Creutzfeldt-Jakob: morre aos 59 anos moradora de SC | G1

articles.summary: Rose Carvalho, de Gaspar (SC), convivia com os sintomas da Creutzfeldt-Jakob há mais de dois anos. O marido, Luís da Silva, saiu do emprego para cuidar dela.
articles.body:
Adicione o g1 como Fonte Preferida no Google

Rose Carvalho, moradora de Gaspar (SC) que convivia com Creutzfeldt-Jakob, morreu nesta terça-feira (24), aos 59 anos. A doença rara e degenerativa é a mesma que causou a morte do influenciador Lito , em outubro deste ano, e é caracterizada pela perda de movimentos e demência.

A morte foi confirmada em uma publicação no perfil das redes sociais criado pela família para compartilhar atualizações sobre o estado de saúde de Rose.

Rose recebeu o diagnóstico em 2024 e chegou a perder os movimentos e a fala.

O marido, Luís da Silva, de 61 anos, contou ao g1 que deixou o emprego para cuidar de Rose. O casal estava junto há 19 anos. Ele fazia questão de manter a rotina com as atividades favoritas da esposa.

🔎 A doença de Creutzfeldt-Jakob é rara, neurodegenerativa, progressiva e sem cura. O quadro costuma começar com demência, perda de memória e tremores, e evolui com outros sinais neurológicos que afetam diferentes regiões do cérebro simultaneamente.

Rose começou a sentir sintomas, vertigens e tonturas em fevereiro de 2024. A princípio, a família suspeitava de labirintite. Porém, o quadro dela evoluiu rapidamente.

Ela passou a ter dificuldades para falar, perdeu o equilíbrio e começou a sofrer quedas frequentes. Para obter o diagnóstico, a paciente passou por diversas consultas e exames.

O diagnóstico da doença de Creutzfeld-Jakob foi confirmado posteriormente a partir da análise de uma amostra corporal enviada ao Hospital das Clínicas da Universidade de São Paulo (USP).

Antes de falecer, Rose se alimentava por sonda e respirava com o auxílio de uma traqueostomia. Ela já havia perdido os movimentos e a fala.

Rose Carvalho, que agora sofre sintomas da doença Creutzfeld-Jacob, e o marido, Luís da Silva — Foto: Arquivo pessoal

Luís conta que, antes de adoecer, Rose era uma mulher ativa, alegre, sempre disposta a ajudar e apaixonada pela vida.

"Ela era uma força da natureza, muito alegre e afetuosa. Ela adorava música, sair para dançar, encontrar pessoas e dar boas risadas. Ela adorava estar na praia, viajar, e filmes. Ela era uma cinéfila de primeira grandeza", descreveu Luís.

Marido largou emprego para cuidar da esposa

Para se dedicar integralmente à esposa, Luís largou o emprego de chef de cozinha. Ele contou ao g1 que a rotina de cuidados começava por volta das 3h30 e terminava perto das 22h. Durante as madrugadas, ele ainda acordava para verificar o estado de Rose e aspirar secreções acumuladas nos pulmões dela.

Durante o dia, o marido dedicava horas para movimentar o corpo de Rose, que já não se mexia por conta própria. Os exercícios físicos eram feitos para estimular a interação dela.

Em dias ensolarados, ele a levava ao jardim para que ficasse perto das flores, uma das grandes paixões de Rose.

Luís da Silva leva esposa, Rose Carvalho, para passear no jardim junto às flores — Foto: Arquivo pessoal

Trata-se de uma doença priônica — causada pela alteração anormal de uma proteína chamada príon, que se multiplica no cérebro e destrói neurônios, deixando no tecido cerebral um padrão de buracos que dá origem ao termo "espongiforme". A enfermidade é rara, progressiva e, até hoje, sem tratamento capaz de reverter ou interromper sua evolução.

Mais de 85% dos casos são da chamada forma esporádica, sem causa e fonte infecciosa conhecida, de acordo com o Ministério da Saúde . Geralmente acomete pessoas com média de idade de 65 anos e já foram relatados casos em pessoas entre os 14 aos 92 anos de idade.

Entre 5% e 15% dos casos são hereditários. Nos demais, menos de 1%, a proteína anormal é transmitida de forma acidental.

Não há cura. Aproximadamente 90% das pessoas acometidas pela doença morrem em um ano.

Segundo levantamento do Ministério da Saúde, o Brasil registrou 547 casos confirmados da enfermidade entre 2005 e 2021 — período que corresponde aos primeiros 17 anos desde que a doença de Creutzfeldt-Jakob passou a integrar a lista de notificações compulsórias.

articles.title: Tentativa de feminicídio em Monteiro: réu é condenado por crime | G1
articles.standfirst: Rossana Queiroz ficou dois meses em coma após as agressões, em 2022, e convive com sequelas; julgamento aconteceu nesta terça-feira (24).
articles.summary: Tentativa de feminicídio em Monteiro termina com condenação de réu que agrediu Rossana Queiroz em 2022, deixando a vítima com sequelas motoras e de fala permanentes.
articles.body:
Adicione o g1 como Fonte Preferida no Google

O julgamento de José Anderson da Silva, acusado de tentar matar a ex-namorada, Rossana Queiroz, aconteceu nesta terça-feira (24), em Monteiro , no Cariri da Paraíba. O júri popular começou no início da manhã e terminou por volta das 21h. O réu foi condenado a 15 anos e 7 meses e 15 dias de reclusão regime inicial fechado.

Os crimes imputados contra o réu foram: tentativa de homicídio qualificado e feminicídio. O tribunal também estabeleceu um indenização de R$ 100 mil a vítima.

A tentativa de feminicídio contra a mulher aconteceu na madrugada de 28 de junho de 2022, após uma festa junina na cidade. Segundo informações apresentadas durante o processo, os dois teriam discutido durante a festa e, em seguida, o homem teria seguido a vítima até a residência dela, onde aconteceram as agressões.

Na ocasião, vizinhos ouviram os gritos de Rossana e foram até o imóvel para verificar o que estava acontecendo. Ao chegarem ao local, encontraram a mulher gravemente ferida, caída em uma poça de sangue, enquanto o acusado ainda estaria ao lado dela.

A vítima, que tinha 27 anos na época, sofreu diversas agressões na região da cabeça e teve um traumatismo cranioencefálico. O caso é tratado como tentativa de feminicídio qualificado por motivo fútil e mediante recurso que dificultou a defesa da vítima.

José Anderson da Silva, acusado de tentar matar a ex-namorada, — Foto: Reprodução/TV Cabo Branco

Anderson teve a liberdade provisória concebida no dia 4 de julho de 2022, pela juíza substituta da 1ª vara da comarca de Monteiro. Em 16 de julho de 2022, um novo mandado de prisão foi expedido e cumprido.

Vítima ficou em coma e convive com sequelas

Vítima convive com sequelas após agressões — Foto: Reprodução/Instagram

Em relatos publicados nas redes sociais, Rossana contou que o ex-companheiro bateu a cabeça dela contra a parede e pulou sobre seu corpo várias vezes durante as agressões.

Em decorrência da violência, ela ficou dois meses em coma e precisou passar por um longo processo de recuperação, chegando a ficar sem beber água pela boca, sem comer e sem falar. A mulher também permaneceu internada por aproximadamente quatro meses no Hospital de Emergência e Trauma de Campina Grande.

Atualmente, Rossana convive com sequelas que comprometeram sua fala e locomoção. Entre as consequências está a paralisia espástica, condição que provoca rigidez muscular e reflexos exagerados. O quadro pode estar associado a lesões nas vias motoras do cérebro.

O julgamento estava inicialmente previsto para 26 de outubro, mas foi adiado após um pedido da defesa. Na ocasião, José Anderson não teria aceitado ser representado por um defensor público.

A sessão foi remarcada para esta terça-feira (24), em Monteiro. A defesa do acusado também chegou a solicitar a transferência do julgamento para outra cidade, sob o argumento de que a repercussão do caso poderia interferir na decisão dos jurados. O pedido não foi aceito, e o júri popular foi mantido no município onde o crime aconteceu.

Durante o julgamento, Rossana foi ouvida, assim como testemunhas do caso, a defensoria publica e o réu.

articles.title: Rekha shows improvement, starts speaking, but docs favour ICU observation
articles.summary: BJP Hingalganj MLA Rekha Patra shows improvement after suspected poisoning, off ventilator and speaking; doctors keep her in ICU amid lung risk.
articles.body: Kolkata: BJP’s Hingalganj MLA Rekha Patra’s health condition showed considerable improvement by Tuesday afternoon, with her slurred speech reducing significantly and her ability to communicate returning.However, doctors are yet to rule out complications arising from suspected poisoning and have decided to keep her in ICU for close observation.Patra, who is undergoing treatment at a private hospital off EM Bypass, was taken off ventilator support on Monday and has not required it since. She has started speaking and is able to communicate physical discomfort to doctors, hospital sources said.“She has started speaking a bit. However, doctors are not willing to take any risks right now. They are in favour of keeping the MLA in ICU,” said Archana Das Majumdar, a state BJP neta and close associate of Patra.Although her overall condition has improved, Patra continues to receive supplemental oxygen. Hospital sources said other clinical parameters had also shown encouraging signs of recovery.Doctors, however, remain concerned about possible lung complications following the suspected poisoning. Excessive salivation had reportedly caused some secretions to enter her lungs when she was not fully conscious, affecting the smooth supply of oxygen to her body.Meanwhile, doctors are yet to establish the exact composition of the suspected poison detected in her stomach. articles.title: Unvaccinated Pennsylvania resident dies of measles in state's ninth fatal case this year
articles.summary: Pennsylvania officials say an unvaccinated Centre County resident died of measles, the ninth death this year, as the state leads the nation in cases.
articles.body: Pennsylvania health officials announced Monday that a resident unvaccinated against measles died from the virus after testing positive, making it the ninth measles-related death in the state this year. The Pennsylvania Department of Health confirmed the death less than a week after the United States lost its measles elimination status, ending a public health achievement that had been maintained since 2000. Officials said the victim was a resident of Centre County, located in the middle of the state and most known for being home to Penn State University. The state has 1,638 confirmed measles cases across 46 counties this year, including 49 new infections that were reported Monday. CHILD’S MEASLES DEATH MARKS NEW YORK STATE’S FIRST IN MORE THAN 30 YEARS AMID OUTBREAK Hospitalizations rose from 315 to 330, according to the state’s measles dashboard. Just five of the confirmed infections involved vaccinated residents. Last week, officials confirmed the state’s eighth measles death, an unvaccinated Clinton County resident. Pennsylvania and federal health authorities continue to urge residents to get the measles, mumps and rubella (MMR) vaccine, saying it the best defense against the disease. Pennsylvania has been battling a measles outbreak since April and now leads the nation in cases, accounting for more than a quarter of all U.S. infections. TRUMP SURGEON GENERAL PICK BACKS MMR VACCINE, REJECTS LINK BETWEEN CHILDHOOD VACCINES AND AUTISM The sharp rise in cases — largely in rural and Amish communities with historically low vaccination rates — has prompted state health officials to ramp up immunization efforts. The state health department has administered more than 7,400 doses of the MMR vaccine at nearly 300 pop-up clinics. Officials plan to set up dozens more of these temporary immunization sites over the coming weeks and months. For months, Pennsylvania Governor Josh Shapiro and Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. have sparred over the response to the ongoing measles outbreak in the state. Shapiro has accused Kennedy of spreading misinformation about the MMR vaccine and vaccines in general, something the nation's top health official has denied. AMISH FACE NEW YORK VACCINE MANDATE IN SUPREME COURT FIGHT, MIGHT HAVE TO ‘PACK THEIR WAGONS’ Overall, Kennedy has given a mix of answers about his stance on the MMR vaccine. When testifying before the House in May 2025, he said he would "probably" vaccinate his children against measles. When he was asked the same question in August 2024, prior to becoming HHS secretary, Kennedy said he would not give his kids the MMR vaccine. Kennedy, meanwhile, has accused Shapiro of politicizing the outbreak and suggested that some of Pennsylvania’s reported measles deaths may have been "fabricated." CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP The Pan American Health Organization’s decision last Wednesday to revoke the U.S.’ measles elimination status means the virus is once again considered endemic in the country. This means it is circulating regularly at a relatively predictable level, much like the seasonal flu and chickenpox. The difference is, measles is around 12 times more contagious than the flu and twice as contagious as chickenpox, according to Unicef. People infected with measles — especially babies and young children — also face the risk of severe complications, including a weakened immune system or encephalitis, a type of brain swelling that can cause seizures and intellectual disabilities.

articles.title: GTA 6 gamers warned about new McDonald's ordering feature on Discord
articles.summary: As Grand Theft Auto VI launches, McDonald's adds an "Order McDonald's" Discord feature for McDelivery via Uber Eats, but experts warn of distracted eating.
articles.body: Right on the bumper of the Grand Theft Auto VI (GTA 6) video game release, McDonald's has launched a food ordering feature within Discord, an app widely used among gamers to talk with each other while playing. Now, those who are still in the midst of a GTA 6 marathon can stay fueled up without too much disruption by utilizing an "Order McDonald's" option in Discord that allows players to get McDelivery through Uber Eats, entertainment outlet IGN reported. The integration, which also includes a game called Fast-Lane Feast, is available in the Apps section of all Discord servers, channels and direct messages. 'GRAND THEFT AUTO VI' MANIA COMES WITH SERIOUS HEALTH RISKS, DOCTORS WARN While players won't need to get up from their couch, they will probably have to pause their game, as the food ordering is done through an external Uber Eats link, IGN noted. Fox News Digital reached out to McDonald's for comment. The add-on has a few red flags in the eyes of some healthcare experts. FORMER MCDONALD'S EXEC SPILLS THE BEANS ON WHY HEALTHIER MENU FAVORITE GOT THE AXE "Making food ordering part of a gaming platform adds convenience, but it also raises questions about how food marketing and distracted eating intersect," Geremy Kerr, an Ohio-based registered dietitian, told Fox News Digital. "Eating while absorbed in a game can make it easier to lose track of how much you've eaten." A McDonald's Big Mac meal with a medium fry and medium Coca-Cola contains 1,170 calories, according to the company's website. CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR LIFESTYLE NEWSLETTER "For gamers, a practical approach is to take a break for meals, decide what and how much to order before returning to the game and keep water within reach," Kerr said. "I play video games myself and enjoy comfort food at times, but I still make a point of carving out time in my schedule for exercise and my health, because enjoyment and wellness don't have to be at odds." The new feature arrives at a time when a growing number of young Americans are getting diabetes diagnoses. CLICK HERE FOR MORE LIFESTYLE NEWS By 2060, an estimated 220,000 kids and teens are predicted to be diagnosed with type 2 diabetes, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) recently reported. It's possible to delay or prevent type 2 diabetes by making healthy lifestyle choices, according to the CDC. "Gaming often means hours of sitting, and when comfort food is only a click away without ever pausing the game, the line between leisure and an unhealthy habit gets even thinner," Dr. Swapnil Patel, vice chair of medicine at Jersey Shore University Medical Center in New Jersey, told Fox News Digital. TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ "In excess, that combination can contribute to obesity, high cholesterol and type 2 diabetes." However, that doesn't mean that someone needs to stop gaming altogether, Patel added. "I play video games myself and enjoy comfort food at times, but I still make a point of carving out time in my schedule for exercise and my health, because enjoyment and wellness don't have to be at odds," Patel said. articles.title: GLP-1 Weight-Loss Drugs Tied to Higher Breast Density in New Study. What Women Need to Know
articles.summary: Women who take GLP-1 weight-loss drugs may have denser breasts after being on the treatment, a study finds. Doctors share what it means for breast cancer risk.
articles.body: Women who take popular GLP-1 weight-loss drugs may discover they have increased breast density after being on the anti-obesity treatment, a new study has found. When researchers at the Mass General Brigham Cancer Institute examined the mammograms of 104 women right before they started taking GLP-1 medications like Zepbound and Wegovy and then at least one year after, the scans showed almost two-thirds of the women, 62%, had denser breasts on the follow-up test. The findings have not yet been published in a peer-reviewed journal and will be presented at the annual meeting of the Radiological Society of North America, which starts on Sunday, Nov. 29. The increased breast density is not a direct effect of the GLP-1 medication, but rather the effect of the weight loss, said Dr. Eva Gombos, the study co-author and a radiologist at Mass General Brigham. The women in the study all had obesity before they started treatment and lost 40 pounds on average. “When someone loses substantial weight, fat loss can change the appearance of the face. The same is true for the breast,” Gombos tells TODAY.com. Breasts are composed of fatty tissue and more dense fibroglandular tissue. As breast fat decreases, the fibroglandular tissue in the breast then becomes more prominent on a mammogram, she notes. “The general appearance is more dense, but it shouldn’t cause alarm. It’s just manifestation of the weight loss,” Gombos says. The researchers didn’t demonstrate increased breast cancer risk, she emphasizes. Still, there were some consequences — 22% of the patients in the study were called back for additional screening, and four underwent biopsies, which were all benign. For screening mammograms, it’s normal for patients to get called back for additional testing about 10% of the time, and the rate was double that in this study, which is very high, says Dr. Kimberly Feigin, a radiologist at Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center, who was not involved in the new research. “I think what’s happening is that there may not have been good communication of why the breast density was increasing,” Feigin notes. “Maybe they could have avoided some of the callbacks if (the radiologists) had known that the patient had been on a GLP-1 and had lost a lot of weight.” Dense Breasts and Cancer Risk About half of women who are 40 or older have dense breasts, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. It’s not something a person can see or feel, but is determined by a mammogram. Women with dense breasts have a higher chance of developing breast cancer, the CDC notes. Having dense breasts also makes it harder to find a tumor on a mammogram because both look white on the scan. But Feigin doesn’t believe greater breast density associated with weight loss due to a GLP-1 drug increases a woman’s risk of getting breast cancer. Dr. Elisa Port, breast surgery chief at Mount Sinai Health System, agreed. “The flip side could be true, in fact. We know that being overweight or obese can increase a woman’s risk of breast cancer, so the GLPs may actually be beneficial in overall reducing the risk,” Port said on TODAY. All mammogram facilities across the U.S. are required to notify patients about the density of their breasts. Breast density is fluid — it can change from year to year, says Dr. Eleonora Teplinsky, the head of breast and gynecologic medical oncology at Valley Health System in Paramus, New Jersey. Many studies show it can increase with weight loss in general, she adds, not just with GLP-1s. “My takeaway from this study would be that women who are on a GLP-1 should know that their breast density might change, and they should pay attention to that on their mammogram,” says Teplinsky, who was not involved in the new research. “If they notice a change in their breast density, really talking to their medical teams about what this means for their screening. So do they need to add supplemental imaging with ultrasound or MRI.” Teplinsky doesn’t believe simply being on a GLP-1 should change breast cancer screening at this point. As of now, there’s no need to change any screening recommendation, Gombos agreed. Mammogram Tips If You Are Taking a GLP-1 Gombos encourages women to keep a normal breast cancer screening schedule, which is one mammogram per year. Before getting a mammogram, tell the technologist you are taking a GLP-1 drug so the radiologist will keep that in mind when reading the X-ray, she says. “Make sure that the radiologist is aware of the interval weight loss because the mammogram will look different, and that can help the radiologist interpret the mammogram appropriately,” Feigin adds. If you’re notified that your breasts have suddenly become dense, don’t get alarmed, Gombos says. Be prepared the radiologist may want to get more pictures. “There’s no reason to panic and there’s still very low risk of having cancer,” Port said. Ask your doctor about getting supplemental screening such as a breast ultrasound or breast MRI, Feigin says.

articles.title: ‘Shocking’ drop in hep B vaccination, including babies with infected mothers
articles.summary: Fewer newborns are being vaccinated against hepatitis B, an incurable infection that can lead to liver disease, a large new analysis has found.
articles.body: Fewer newborns are being vaccinated against hepatitis B, an incurable infection that can lead to liver disease, including babies whose mothers are known to have the virus, a large new analysis has found. As of June, just 66% of newborns got the hepatitis B vaccine within a day of their birth, down from 80% in 2022. The birth dose serves as a safety net especially for babies whose pregnant mothers are unaware they’re infected with the virus and unknowingly transmit it during childbirth. Up to 90% of babies with the virus develop chronic infections, putting them at risk for liver failure and liver cancer later in life. Vaccinating them at birth dramatically lowers those odds. The new study from Truveta, a health care and analytics company, included medical records from more than 1.3 million babies born in the United States from January 2018 through June this year. During that time period, newborn vaccination rates increased from 76% in 2018 to 80% in 2022 before declining in mid-2023, falling to 66% by June this year. “It’s shocking to see a nearly 15% decline in three years,” said Nina Masters, lead author and principal applied research scientist at Truveta. “Infants born to mothers with hepatitis B have a 90% chance of perinatal infection. That can mean a lifetime of chronic liver disease, cirrhosis and early death. This is a real preventable tragedy.” The decline began before federal vaccine advisers voted in December to abandon a decades-old recommendation that all babies be vaccinated against hepatitis B at birth. (That decision was later halted by a federal judge in response to a lawsuit filed by the American Academy of Pediatrics. The block remains in effect.) The findings mirror increasing trends in anti-vaccine behavior in general. A recent NBC News data investigation found three-quarters of U.S. counties that track kindergarten immunization rates no longer meet the minimum threshold to prevent measles outbreaks. Now, measles outbreaks are popping up nationwide, with nearly 6,000 cases and at least 13 deaths, according to state health departments. The U.S. lost its measles elimination status Nov. 16, reversing one of the country’s greatest public health achievements this century. “We talk about measles being the canary in the coal mine. We’re seeing those outbreaks,” said Dr. Richard Besser, a pediatrician and president of the Robert Wood Johnson Foundation. “This one — hepatitis B and the rise in unvaccinated newborns — these are the kinds of things that are silent, that you don’t see for years and years until these babies grow up and end up having liver disease.” The study, published Tuesday in NEJM Evidence, also revealed that hepatitis B vaccination rates have fallen among babies born to mothers known to be infected with the virus. Up to 98% of those babies were vaccinated between 2018 through 2025. But between January and June, that rate dropped to 94%. Cases of acute hepatitis B fell dramatically in children after the the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention began recommending a universal birth dose in 1991, falling 99% from 1990 to 2019. A CDC analysis of children born from 1994 to 2023 estimated that hepatitis B vaccination prevented more than 6 million infections and nearly 1 million hospitalizations. Last year, the University of Minnesota’s Vaccine Integrity Project published a review of more than 400 studies, finding no evidence of short- or long-term health problems from the hepatitis B shot after birth. “Reversing the successes of previous public health programs puts individuals’ lives at risk,” Dr. James Conway, a pediatric infectious disease physician and medical director of the UW Health Immunization Program in Madison, Wisconsin, wrote in an email. “It’s sad, tragic and preventable.”

articles.title: Wife of Man Diagnosed With 2 Types of Dementia Recalls First Symptoms: ‘It Wasn’t Obvious’
articles.summary: Mixed dementia is under-diagnosed, research shows. One man has lived with Lewy body dementia and Alzheimer’s for 18 years shares his early symptoms and journey so far.
articles.body: Dementia is one of the most prevalent age-related chronic diseases. The condition, which impairs memory and thinking, can be caused by different neurodegenerative disorders. The most common is Alzheimer’s disease, followed by Lewy body dementia, vascular dementia and frontotemporal dementia. Increasingly, older adults are being diagnosed with more than one type simultaneously, known as “mixed dementia.” The death of actor Patrick Stewart recently put the condition in the spotlight. Stewart died last month at 86 following a brief battle with Alzheimer’s and Lewy body dementia. New research suggests that mixed dementia is much more common than previously recognized, per the Alzheimer’s Association. “We’re just starting to learn more about it, and every person is different, so the rate at which these conditions progress varies extraordinarily, from six months in some people up to 20-plus years in others,” Dr. Sami Barmada, associate professor of neurology at University of Michigan Medicine, tells TODAY.com. Terry of Kentville, Nova Scotia, who asked that his last name be omitted for privacy, has been living with Lewy body dementia for 18 years. The 73-year-old was diagnosed in his fifties, but wouldn’t learn he had Alzheimer’s until nearly a decade later. As doctors become more aware of mixed dementia and people live longer, diagnoses are rising. However, the early symptoms can be hard to recognize. Sleep Disturbances and Tiredness “Terry’s journey with Lewy body dementia began in the fall of 2007. The changes in his behavior, late afternoon tiredness and sleep disturbances were things that we thought were part of the aging process,” Terry’s wife Janet, 74, tells TODAY.com. Sleep problems are a classic symptom of Lewy body dementia — specifically, rapid eye movement sleep disorder, which causes people to act out their dreams in their sleep, per the Mayo Clinic. “It wasn’t obvious to us,” Janet notes. Eventually, Terry could only sleep for an hour at a time. During the day, he was exhausted and anxious. Then, the hallucinations began, causing Terry to see shapes or animals that weren’t there. In 2008, a neurologist diagnosed Terry with Lewy body dementia. He was 54. “They felt as though he already had it for some period of time,” says Janet. The early warning signs can vary significantly. “The best indicator is a change from what somebody was like weeks or months ago,” says Barmada. Often, it’s not the person with dementia who notices the change. “It’s important for people to listen to the observations of their spouses or families or friends, because we don’t always have the best impression of ourselves,” Barmada adds. Lewy Body Dementia and Alzheimer’s Lewy body dementia occurs when a protein called alpha-synuclein builds up into clumps, aka Lewy bodies, inside the nerve cells in the brain, Barmada explains. This causes the neurons to malfunction and die. It affects cognitive abilities along with movement, sleep and the autonomic nervous system, per the Mayo Clinic. “In 2016, Terry had more tests and (doctors thought) he had Alzheimer’s. We didn’t know you could have both together,” says Janet. Alzheimer’s is also caused by a buildup of proteins — amyloid beta and tau proteins — which form plaques that damage the brain, says Barmada. This affects cognition, primarily causing memory loss. Lewy body dementia and Alzheimer’s are both progressive, which means they gradually worsen over time as the neurons die. Most cases are not genetic, but are instead caused by a combination of aging, lifestyle and environmental factors. Although Terry’s brother died from Lewy body disease, it rarely affects more than one family member, per the National Institutes of Health. Lewy body dementia is often misdiagnosed as Alzheimer’s in the early stages. Accurate diagnosis is key, because some Alzheimer’s medications can worsen Lewy body dementia, per the Lewy Body Dementia Association. Living with Mixed Dementia During the first 10 years of living with Lewy body dementia, Terry remained active. He could drive and play golf. By 2018, his hallucinations became so severe that he gave up his driver’s license. Today, Terry often uses a walker. “He has more balance issues and falls. Swallowing foods or digesting foods also became a bigger issue,” says Janet. While Terry has retained his long-term memory, his short-term memory is now “non-existent” due to Alzheimer’s, she adds. The couple, however, still makes an effort to find joy in simple things, like enjoying a cup of coffee. “You’ve got to realize that you’re going to die. So you try to make the best of what you can at the time,” Terry tells TODAY.com. One of the biggest challenges is how others treat his diagnosis. “You know who your friends are. When first you get diagnosed, they say, ‘Oh, you look wonderful today,’ but when you’re in really bad shape, eventually they kind of dissipate away. I find that really frustrating,” Terry says. “The hardest part is when people hear you have dementia, they kind of avoid you,” Janet adds. A misconception the couple deals with often is that dementia always causes aggression. “Terry is one of the ones that isn’t aggressive. He’s more fearful,” says Janet. The couple wishes people had more empathy and compassion for dementia patients. “Before all this started, he was a confident, successful individual, and this has changed everything,” she adds. One silver lining of the diagnosis is that it led them to adopt a dog, which acts as a therapy and companion animal for Terry. Treatment and Research There is no cure for Lewy body dementia or Alzheimer’s, but certain therapies can help manage symptoms. No drugs are approved by the U.S. Food and Drug Administration to treat mixed dementia, per the Alzheimer’s Association. Some medications approved to treat Alzheimer’s may be prescribed for Lewy body dementia, depending on the patient. “Terry’s got a list of three pages of medications he can’t take because Lewy body dementia causes so many sensitivities. So he’s not on very much,” says Janet. Lifestyle interventions can also help improve the quality of life. “We have a certain routine we stick to. We try to be outside as much as we can, and we do dementia activity books,” says Janet. “Every day needs to include humor, music and positive thoughts,” she adds. Terry is also a participant at the Michigan Alzheimer’s Disease Research Center. “We’re still looking for answers, and one of the things that has provided an incredible amount of information about (mixed dementia) is brain donation,” says Barmada. Autopsies allow doctors to observe physical changes in the brain caused by dementia, which are difficult to measure in living individuals, per the Alzheimer’s Association. Terry and Janet have agreed to donate to the University of Michigan’s Brain Bank. The Importance of Caregivers “The caregiver is one of the most critical factors in how quickly a disease progresses,” says Barmada. Dementia impacts a person’s ability to care for themselves. “It’s those people who have good caregivers in place that are able to take advantage of the support and, despite the progression of their disease, live longer,” Barmada adds. Caregiving responsibilities often fall onto family members. Janet retired early five years ago to care for Terry full-time, and plans to do so for as long as possible. It’s a rewarding job, but also incredibly challenging. “I keep dough in the freezer, and on days when I feel really warped, I pound it for a few minutes. It sounds crazy, but it relieves the tension,” Janet says. Joining support groups has helped her find a community. “Caregivers need to find rest and care for themselves, because if they do not take care of themselves, they cannot take care of their loved ones,” she says. November is National Family Caregivers Month. If you or a loved one is struggling with dementia, call the Alzheimer Association’s free 24/7 helpline (800.272.3900) for support.

articles.title: Popular actor says bladder cancer discovery followed one strange bathroom symptom
articles.summary: Jonathan Frakes says the sight of pink urine led to a cystoscopy and a high-grade non-muscle-invasive bladder cancer diagnosis caught in time.
articles.body: For "Star Trek: The Next Generation" star Jonathan Frakes, a life-altering health scare began not with physical pain, but with a strange sighting during a regular trip to Phoenix. "My pee was pink," Frakes shared during an episode of his podcast, "Dropping Names with Brent and Jonny," alongside his co-star Brent Spiner and urologic surgeon Dr. Ram Narayanan. "I was unnerved." Searching for an easy explanation, Frakes said he considered blaming his diet. Maybe it was beets, he mused, before realizing he hadn't touched one in six years. MAN GOES TO DOCTOR TO PROVE HE’S 'IN PERFECT SHAPE,' TEST REVEALS SHOCKING DIAGNOSIS Frakes ultimately called his doctor, a decision that may have saved his bladder. According to Narayanan, Frakes experienced what is clinically known as painless gross hematuria, or visible blood in the urine without accompanying pain. "When it’s painless blood that you see with your eyes, that’s always a red flag," the doctor said on the podcast. While blood in the urine can stem from benign causes like urinary tract infections or kidney stones, painless visible hematuria is the most common symptom of bladder cancer. It always warrants an immediate urological evaluation, according to both Cleveland Clinic and the National Institutes of Health (NIH). DIAGNOSTIC TEST COULD FLAG WHICH MEN NEED AGGRESSIVE PROSTATE CANCER TREATMENT AND WHICH DON'T Days after finishing a fan convention, Frakes underwent an in-office cystoscopy, a quick procedure in which a thin camera examines the lining of the bladder. Inside, Narayanan spotted small, fern-like growths. TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ Three days later, Frakes was in the operating room to undergo a blue light cystoscopy — a specialized exam that uses an imaging dye to make hidden tumors glow — and tumor resection to scrape away the abnormal tissue. The biopsy confirmed high-grade, non-muscle-invasive bladder cancer. To illustrate why early timing was so critical, Narayanan compared the bladder to a layer cake — scraping away the surface "icing" removed the tumor before it could invade the deeper muscle wall, which often forces surgeons to remove the entire bladder and fashion a new one from a piece of intestine. "At the end of it, he says, 'I think we got it all,'" Frakes recalled. CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES To prevent the cancer from returning, Frakes underwent six weekly rounds of intravesical therapy, where a liquid medication is placed directly into the bladder. While immunotherapy is the standard first-line treatment, a nationwide shortage led Narayanan to administer a combination of two chemotherapy drugs, gemcitabine and docetaxel. "At the end of it, he says, ‘I think we got it all.’" According to medical experts, this dual-agent chemotherapy has proven to be a highly effective alternative during immunotherapy shortages. While inspecting Frakes’ bladder, Narayanan noticed a secondary issue: an enlarged prostate. As Frakes joked on air, his surgeon told him, "While I was in there, I noticed your prostate is the size of a small town." CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER The enlarged prostate was forcing Frakes’ bladder muscle to work overtime, a condition called trabeculation, which can eventually lead to bladder failure. After ruling out prostate cancer via MRI, Narayanan performed a surgery to remove roughly 135 grams of obstructing tissue through a single tiny incision. As a result, Frakes was able to stop taking his daily prostate medications, and his urinary symptoms vanished. Other than immediate family, the actor kept his diagnosis private until deciding to share his story during Men’s Health Awareness Month to encourage other men to overcome their reluctance to see a urologist, whom Narayanan affectionately calls "primary care doctors below the belt." CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP "If something happens like [what] happened to you, check it out immediately," the doctor urged listeners. "Don't be shy. Don't be afraid."

articles.title: Wisconsin reports 3rd measles death, as illnesses spread to the general public
articles.summary: A third person has died of measles in Wisconsin, state health officials reported Tuesday, as cases across the state soared to 920 since the outbreak began in late summer.
articles.body: A third person has died of measles in Wisconsin, state health officials reported Tuesday, as cases across the state soared to 920 since the outbreak began in late summer. The Wisconsin Department of Health Services said the death occurred in an adult, but declined to provide additional details. Earlier this month, two children with measles died in the state. The state’s outbreak had been concentrated in largely Amish populations in the southwestern corner of Wisconsin, but has now spread into counties in the central and northern part of the state. There are growing signs that cases are spilling over into the general population, said Dr. James Conway, a pediatric infectious disease physician and medical director of the UW Health Immunization Program in Madison, Wisconsin. “What we’ve started to see is pop-up clusters in a number of counties, and not all of them can be directly drawn to the Plain community,” Conway said. “It’s a brush fire turning into a forest fire pretty quickly right before our eyes.” Nearly all of the people who’ve tested positive, 99.2%, were unvaccinated. Twenty people have needed hospitalization. During a media briefing Tuesday, Stephanie Schauer, immunization program manager for the Wisconsin Health Department, said that 14 women have tested positive while pregnant and there’s been one reported case of congenital measles. The state is also requesting a second round of help from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. A CDC team previously deployed to the area in mid-August. “We are going to be receiving additional staff to do case investigation, public communication and management of data,” Wisconsin’s state epidemiologist for communicable diseases, Dr. Ryan Westergaard, said during the meeting. “We decided to do this now, several months into the outbreak, when it became clear that the outbreak was growing rather than shrinking.” Tuesday’s announcement marks the 14th measles death this year, according to a tally from state health departments in New York, Pennsylvania, Virginia and Wisconsin. At least six have been reported in children.

articles.title: Can air pollution cause lung cancer? How long-term exposure to PM2.5, vehicle emissions, industrial fumes and indoor smoke can increase cancer risk, symptoms to watch for and ways to protect your lungs, explained by an oncologist
articles.summary: Lung cancer is often associated with smoking, however, there are many other risk factors including exposure to air pollution and certain environmental and
articles.body: Lung cancer is often associated with smoking, however, there are many other risk factors including exposure to air pollution and certain environmental and occupational substances. As air quality is becoming a concern in many Indian metros, it is important to understand the link between pollution and lung cancer.How is air pollution linked to lung cancer?Air pollution involves many harmful gases and small particles which can enter the respiratory system. Some of the particles are very minute and can enter deep into the lungs causing damage including inflammation and oxidative stress. Particulate matter in the air, specifically PM2.5 is a concern as the particles are small enough to enter the deepest part of the lungs. Long term exposure to air pollution outdoors and particulate matter has been classed as a carcinogen by the international agency for research on cancer (IARC), meaning there is enough evidence to show that outdoor air pollution can increase your risk of lung cancer manifold.However, the risk of developing lung cancer will depend on a number of factors including how long you are exposed to the pollution, levels of exposure, your inherent susceptibility, lifestyle and other environmental factors.Environmental risks that can increase riskOutdoor air pollution is an important environmental risk factor in relation to lung cancer. Car fumes, industrial processes, building dust, burning waste and fossil fuels can all cause poor air quality. Those living in highly polluted urban areas may be exposed to higher levels of pollution for longer periods of time. Indoor air pollution can also cause issues. Smoke from cooking using fuels can cause exposure to harmful substances over a period of years. Tobacco smoke including second and third hand smoke can also be a large risk.Occupational risks may cause increased exposure to carcinogens. Working within industries involving asbestos, diesel exhaust, welding fumes and other industrial chemicals can put those working in these industries at increased risk. This can be increased if proper safety measures aren’t taken.Can non-smokers develop lung cancer due to pollution?Yes! While smoking is the main risk factor for lung cancer, non-smokers can still develop lung cancer. Long term exposure to air pollution, second-hand smoke, radon and certain substances within the workplace can increase your risk.Non-smokers often develop a type of non-small cell lung cancer called adenocarcinoma. Some patients may have specific genetic changes such as EGFR or ALK. Knowing what genetic changes, you may have can help your doctor choose the best targeted therapy. Remember lung cancer doesn’t always relate to smoking and if you are experiencing ongoing symptoms, it is important to seek medical advice.Symptoms to look out forSymptoms of lung cancer can often develop slowly and can mimic common lung issues. Symptoms to look out for include a persistent cough, coughing up blood, unexplained weight loss, chest pain/discomfort, breathlessness and frequent respiratory infections.If your cough changes or isn’t improving with treatment it is important to seek medical advice. These symptoms don’t necessarily mean you have cancer but can help identify the cause of your symptoms so you can get the right treatment as soon as possible.How is lung cancer caused by pollution diagnosed?Your doctor will want to know your full medical history, perform a physical examination and ask about your symptoms and risk factors. Based on this they may want to carry out some imaging such as an x-ray or CT scan of your chest. If they find an abnormality, they may want to carry out further investigations such as a pet CT scan, bronchoscopy or biopsy. A biopsy is usually needed to make a diagnosis. Further genetic testing may be advised to see what genetic changes you have. Low dose CT scans as a screening tool may be advised if you fit into the high-risk criteria (mainly for chronic smokers). However, it is not advised as a general screening tool.Can the risk be reduced?you cannot completely avoid air pollution there are ways to reduce your exposure. Avoid all forms of tobacco, improve ventilation in your home, avoid cooking smoke and follow safety guidelines at work. If the air quality is poor try to avoid spending long periods of time outside, especially near busy roads/building sites. If working in an environment where you are exposed to harmful dust/fumes/chemicals wear properly fitting protective gear.Why it is important to detect lung cancer earlyAir pollution is an important environmental risk factor for lung cancer. While not everyone who is exposed to polluted air will develop lung cancer, long term exposure shouldn’t be ignored. Knowing the symptoms to look out for, knowing your risk factors and seeking medical advice can help detect lung cancer early. To keep your lungs healthy try to avoid exposure to harmful pollutants and raise your awareness.Dr. (Prof.) Vishwanath S, Lead Oncosciences Karnataka region, Senior consultant and academic advisor, Department of medical oncology, Apollo hospitals, Bengaluru
